key_terms.meaning: Opposition of a magnetic path to flux, 𝓡 = l/(μ₀μᵣA), unit ampere-turns per weber (A·t/Wb)
L = N²/𝓡, where N is the number of turns and 𝓡 is the reluctance of the whole flux path (henry)
A coil whose air gap is changed by the measurand, so 𝓡 and hence L change with displacement
Flux linkage in one coil caused by current in another, M = k√(L₁L₂), unit henry
The non-magnetic gap in the magnetic circuit; its reluctance dominates and varies linearly with x
A three-coil inductive transducer whose differential secondary output is proportional to core displacement
The centre coil of an LVDT, excited by AC at 1–10 kHz, typically 3–15 V rms
Two identical coils on either side of the primary, connected in series opposition so outputs subtract
Core position at the exact centre where both secondary EMFs are equal, giving zero differential output
Small non-zero output at null caused by winding and core imperfections, usually under 1% of full-scale output
A rotary inductive device giving an output voltage whose amplitude varies with shaft angle
A pair of wound rotary machines, transmitter and receiver or control transformer, that transmit shaft angle
A small precision rotary variable-reluctance pick-off used for fine angular measurement and rate sensing
Circulating current induced in a conductor by a changing magnetic field, which creates a field that opposes the cause
A non-contact sensor giving a clean ON/OFF output when a target enters its sensing field
The gap between switch-ON distance and switch-OFF distance, expressed as a percentage of nominal sensing range
A sensor using C = ε₀εᵣA/d, where A is plate area, d the gap and εᵣ the dielectric constant
Three-plate arrangement where the moving plate increases one capacitance and decreases the other, giving linear output
A capacitor whose diaphragm moves with sound pressure, changing d and producing a voltage at fixed charge
A sealed capacitor whose diaphragm deflects under pressure, changing the gap and hence capacitance

takeaways: A coil's inductance is set by the reluctance of its magnetic path, so any mechanical movement that changes an air gap becomes a measurable inductance change.
The LVDT gives a differential AC output that is linear, frictionless, and whose phase reverses as the core crosses the null, so magnitude and direction both come out of one device.
Rotary inductive devices such as the induction potentiometer, synchro and microsyn convert shaft angle into a voltage through stator–rotor mutual inductance.
An eddy current transducer reads the impedance change of a coil near a conductor, so it measures gap, conductivity or defects with no contact and no wear.
A proximity sensor is judged by its sensing range, hysteresis, repeatability and switching frequency, and its wiring is chosen as PNP or NPN to match the PLC input.
A capacitive transducer can be built to respond to gap, area or dielectric, and a differential plate arrangement linearises the output and cancels common errors.
Capacitive sensors need charge amplifiers or AC bridges because the capacitance change is tiny, often picofarads.
Microphones and pressure sensors share the same physics: a diaphragm moves one plate of a capacitor, and the gap change becomes a voltage.
bank_note: Long answers are expected on LVDT construction, output characteristics and applications, and on capacitive transducer types with signal conditioning; variable reluctance, synchro, eddy current and proximity sensors appear as shorter or comparison parts, and biomedical uses (pressure, breathing and displacement) are asked with them.

bank.q: Define magnetic reluctance and derive the expression for the inductance of a coil in terms of turns and reluctance. Explain, with a sketch, how a variable reluctance transducer uses an air gap to measure displacement.
outline: 𝓡 = l/(μ₀μᵣA), units A·t/Wb
Flux Φ = NI/𝓡, linkage NΦ, so L = N²/𝓡
Air gap dominates reluctance because μᵣ of air is 1 against thousands for iron
Gap change gives a large L change; sketch of E-core or plunger type
Output is non-linear with gap; single coil needs a bridge to convert L change to voltage
answer: Reluctance. The opposition a magnetic path offers to flux, the magnetic analogue of resistance: 𝓡 = l/(μ₀μrA), with l the path length (m), A the cross-section (m²), μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m and μr the relative permeability. Unit: ampere-turns per weber (A·t/Wb), the same as H⁻¹.

answer.text: Derivation of L. A coil of N turns carrying current I drives a magnetomotive force NI round the path:
answer.pre:
Flux:          Φ = NI/𝓡
Flux linkage:  λ = NΦ = N²I/𝓡
Inductance:    L = λ/I = N²/𝓡

answer: Series paths. Iron and air gap are in series, so 𝓡 = 𝓡iron + 𝓡gap. With μr of iron in the thousands and μr = 1 for air, a gap of a millimetre outweighs a long iron path.

svg.aria: Sketch of a variable reluctance transducer: a laminated E-shaped iron core with a coil of N turns on the centre leg, and a movable iron armature below it separated by an air gap g; moving the armature changes g. Beside it the formulas L equals N squared over reluctance and L approximately mu zero A N squared over g, with 62.83 millihenry at 1.0 millimetre and 52.36 millihenry at 1.2 millimetre.

answer: How it measures displacement. The armature is fixed to the moving part. Since 𝓡 ≈ g/(μ₀A), L ≈ μ₀AN²/g: a displacement that opens the gap from 1.0 to 1.2 mm lowers L from 62.83 to 52.36 mH, a 16.7 % fall for a 20 % gap change. The coil is one arm of an AC bridge excited at a few kilohertz, and the bridge output amplitude follows the gap.

Characteristics. L ∝ 1/g, so the response is non-linear; sensitivity dL/dg = −μ₀AN²/g² is highest at small gaps (−62.8 mH/mm at 1.0 mm). A differential (push-pull) arrangement with a coil on each side of the armature gives an output (Vs/2)·x/g that is linear and twice as large.
Check. Halving the gap doubles L (125.7 mH at 0.5 mm), confirming L ∝ 1/g; the 5 % iron correction shows why the gap-only formula is an approximation.

bank.q: Draw the construction of an LVDT and explain its working. Why are the two secondaries connected in series opposition, and what happens to the output magnitude and phase as the core moves from below null to above null?
outline: Former, primary at centre, two identical secondaries S₁ and S₂, movable soft-iron core, shield
Primary excited with AC, usually 1–10 kHz
Series opposition so output = e₁ − e₂, zero at null
Core off-centre: nearer secondary has larger EMF, output rises with displacement
Output magnitude proportional to displacement, phase flips by 180° across null
Graph of output vs displacement: linear between about ±0.25 to ±0.4 of full range
answer: Construction. (i) A hollow insulating former. (ii) A primary winding at its centre. (iii) Two identical secondaries S₁ and S₂ wound symmetrically on either side. (iv) A soft-iron or nickel-iron core that slides inside without touching, fixed by a non-magnetic rod to the moving part. (v) A magnetic shield and earthed case against stray fields.

svg.aria: LVDT cross-section: an insulating former with secondary 1 on the left, the primary in the centre and secondary 2 on the right, and a soft-iron core displaced by x towards secondary 1, attached to a push rod. The secondaries are in series opposition so the output is V1 minus V2.

answer: Working. The primary is excited with AC, typically 3–15 V rms at 1–10 kHz. The core carries the primary flux into the two secondaries, which receive voltages V₁ and V₂ by mutual induction. The flux each one links depends on how much of the core lies inside it.

Why series opposition. Connecting S₁ and S₂ so that their voltages subtract gives Vout = V₁ − V₂: zero at the centre and growing with displacement. Connected aiding, the output would be V₁ + V₂, which stays almost constant: in the chapter’s example V₁ + V₂ = 1.80 + 1.80 = 3.60 V at null and 2.00 + 1.60 = 3.60 V at 0.80 mm, so it carries no information. Opposition also cancels drifts that affect both secondaries equally.

answer.text: Output as the core moves from below null to above null (K = 0.50 V/mm, 5 V rms excitation):

answer: Magnitude and phase. The magnitude falls linearly to (nearly) zero as the core approaches null and rises linearly beyond it, a V-shaped curve. The phase jumps by 180° at null. A phase-sensitive demodulator multiplies the output by the excitation reference and gives a signed DC voltage, so the V becomes a straight line through zero.

Linear range. The output is linear while the core ends stay well inside the two secondaries, roughly the middle part of the travel; beyond that the curve flattens. Linearity is typically ±0.1 % to ±0.5 % of full scale.

Residual voltage. At null a few millivolts remain from winding mismatch, harmonics of the excitation and capacitive coupling; much of it is in quadrature and the phase-sensitive demodulator rejects it.

Applications. Displacement and thickness gauging, position feedback in servo valves and machine slides, pressure (a diaphragm or Bourdon tube moves the core), and in biomechanics the extension of bone and tendon specimens.
Check. 0.40 V ÷ 0.50 V/mm = 0.80 mm, and the sign comes only from the phase: magnitude alone gives 0.80 mm on either side.

bank.q: Explain the construction and principle of operation of an induction potentiometer and a synchro transmitter. State two applications of each.
outline: Induction potentiometer: rotor winding and distributed stator winding, mutual inductance varies with rotor angle
Output amplitude follows a sine or cosine of shaft angle; single-phase AC excitation
Synchro: three-phase stator with 120° spaced windings, single-phase rotor
Rotor angle sets stator flux pattern, so the three stator voltages identify the shaft angle
Applications: angular position, remote indication, control transformer in servo loops
answer: Induction potentiometer: construction. A rotary transformer. The stator carries a winding distributed over many slots; the rotor carries a single concentrated winding fed through slip rings. Both are wound on laminated iron with a small, uniform air gap.

Principle. The rotor is excited with AC, Ex. The mutual inductance between rotor and stator depends on the angle between their magnetic axes. Measuring θ from electrical zero (axes at 90°, minimum coupling), the stator voltage is eo = k·Ex·sin θ, with k < 1 the coupling constant. Near zero, sin θ ≈ θ, so the output is linear in angle; its phase reverses across zero.

Numbers. k = 0.5, Ex = 10 V rms: at 10°, eo = 0.868 V (linear law 0.873 V, 0.5 % high); at 30°, eo = 2.500 V (linear law 2.618 V, 4.7 % high). So the device is used over a few tens of degrees, and a 5 mV null voltage limits resolution to about 0.06°.

Synchro transmitter: construction. Like a small alternator: a single-phase rotor (salient-pole, dumbbell shaped) on the input shaft, fed through slip rings, and a stator with three identical windings whose axes are 120° apart, star connected.

Principle. The rotor excitation Er (typically 26 V or 115 V rms) induces in each stator coil a voltage proportional to the cosine of the angle between rotor axis and coil axis: K·Er·cos θ, K·Er·cos(θ − 120°), K·Er·cos(θ + 120°). All three are in time phase (or antiphase) with the excitation; their amplitudes form a pattern that is unique for each θ in 360°.

answer.text: Numbers. 6.81 V rms maximum per coil, rotor at 30°:

answer: Transmitting the angle. The three stator leads are wired to a synchro receiver, which turns its rotor to the same angle, or to a control transformer, whose rotor gives an error voltage e = Emax·sin Δθ. With Emax = 10 V and Δθ = 10°, e = 1.74 V rms, which a servo amplifier uses to turn the load until Δθ = 0.

head: Device
Two applications
rows: valve-stem or damper angle indication; angle feedback in slow servo loops
remote indication of antenna, rudder or gun-turret angle; control transformer as the error detector of an AC position servo

answer: Check. The three stator voltages sum to zero (5.90 + 0 − 5.90), as they must for windings 120° apart.

bank.q: Explain the principle of an eddy current transducer. How do coil impedance, gap and target conductivity affect the reading, and what are its practical applications?
outline: Coil driven by AC, alternating field induces eddy currents in nearby conductor
Eddy currents create an opposing field, changing coil impedance (L and R)
Impedance change depends on gap, conductivity, permeability and frequency
Higher frequency gives a shallower penetration (skin depth)
Applications: displacement, vibration, thickness of foil, crack detection, conductivity sorting
Non-contact, no wear, but only works on conductors
answer: Principle. A probe coil driven with AC (hundreds of kilohertz to a few megahertz) sets up an alternating field. In a conducting target near the probe this field induces emfs, which drive closed loops of current: eddy currents. By Lenz’s law their own field opposes the coil field.

Effect on coil impedance. The coil impedance is Z = R + jωL. Eddy currents take energy from the field, which appears as a rise in the coil’s effective resistance R, and their opposing flux lowers its effective inductance L. For a magnetic target such as steel, the high permeability raises L at the same time, so the net change differs.

Effect of gap (lift-off). The closer the target, the more of the field it intercepts, so the changes in R and L grow as the gap shrinks. Over a range comparable to the coil diameter, the demodulated output is close to linear: in the chapter’s probe, 6.0 V at 1.0 mm with −2.5 V/mm, 4.5 V at 1.6 mm and 3.0 V at 2.2 mm.

Effect of conductivity and frequency. Higher conductivity gives stronger eddy currents. The field penetrates to the skin depth δ = √(2ρ/(ωμ)): aluminium 0.259 mm at 100 kHz and 0.082 mm at 1 MHz; stainless steel 1.35 mm at 100 kHz. A target thinner than about 3δ lets field through, so its thickness changes the reading. The same gap therefore gives different volts on aluminium, brass and steel; calibration is material-specific.

Signal chain. Oscillator → probe coil in a bridge with a reference coil → amplifier → demodulator → filtered DC proportional to gap. A phase-sensitive demodulator separates lift-off from conductivity changes, which rotate the impedance in different directions.

head: Use
What changes
rows: gap to the rotating shaft, at tens of kilohertz bandwidth
Thickness of foil or of a nonconductive coating
coating adds to lift-off; thin foil changes the eddy current depth
a crack interrupts eddy current paths

answer: Merits and limits. No contact and no wear; works through oil, dust and water; fast. It needs a conducting target, the range is short (a few millimetres for a 5 mm coil), and each material needs its own calibration.
Check. On the calibration line an output of 4.5 V gives g = 1.0 + (6.0 − 4.5)/2.5 = 1.6 mm, and the sign of the slope says the output falls as the gap opens.

bank.q: Explain the principle of a capacitive transducer. Describe the three ways its capacitance can change and the signal-conditioning circuits used to convert the change into a voltage.
outline: C = ε₀εᵣA/d with terms defined
Gap-changing type: C varies as 1/d, non-linear
Area-changing type: C varies linearly with overlap area
Dielectric-changing type: used for level and moisture
Differential three-plate capacitor linearises output and cancels common effects
Signal conditioning: AC bridge, charge amplifier, op-amp oscillator/demodulator circuits
High impedance, needs guarding and shielding against stray capacitance
answer: Principle. C = ε₀εrA/d, with ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, εr the relative permittivity of the gap, A the overlapping area (m²) and d the gap (m). Make one of d, A or εr follow the measurand and C carries the reading.

1. Variable gap. A diaphragm or plate moves, C ∝ 1/d. Plates of 100 mm² at 0.50 mm give 1.771 pF; at 0.40 mm 2.214 pF, +25 % for a 20 % gap change: sensitive but non-linear. Used for small displacement, pressure and sound.

2. Variable area. One plate slides across the other at fixed d, C ∝ A, so the output is linear. Plates 5 mm wide at 0.5 mm spacing change by ε₀w/d = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 5 × 10⁻³/0.5 × 10⁻³ = 0.0885 pF per mm of overlap. Used for larger linear and angular displacement.

3. Variable dielectric. A material of different εr fills part of the gap: liquid level (water εr ≈ 80, air 1), sheet thickness, and humidity (a polymer film whose εr follows moisture, as in incubator humidity sensors). For a level probe the wet and dry parts are capacitors in parallel, so C is linear in level.

Differential (three-plate) form. A centre plate between two fixed plates gives C₁ = ε₀A/(d − x), C₂ = ε₀A/(d + x), and (C₁ − C₂)/(C₁ + C₂) = x/d exactly. With d = 0.50 mm and x = 0.05 mm: 1.968 and 1.610 pF, ratio 0.100. It linearises the gap type and cancels common temperature effects.

Signal conditioning 1: AC bridge. The sensor is one arm (or, differential, two arms with a transformer ratio arm) of a bridge excited at 1–100 kHz. Output (Vs/2)·x/d: at 10 V and x/d = 0.1, 0.50 V rms. A phase-sensitive demodulator turns it into signed DC, and a low-pass filter removes the carrier.

Signal conditioning 2: charge amplifier. A bias or polarising voltage Vp on the sensor and an op-amp with feedback capacitor Cf: |Vout| = Vp·ΔC/Cf. The input is a virtual ground, so cable capacitance has almost no signal across it.

Signal conditioning 3: oscillator. The sensor sets the frequency of an oscillator; with L = 1 mH and C = 100 pF, f = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 503.3 kHz, and +1 pF gives 500.8 kHz. A frequency counter or a frequency-to-voltage converter reads it; this suits proximity and level switches.

Guarding and shielding. Sensor capacitances are a few picofarads, so a metre of cable (about 100 pF) would swamp them. Guard rings around the plate and a driven shield on the cable, held at the plate’s potential, stop stray capacitance from carrying signal current. Short leads and stable temperature are part of the design.
Check. The variable-gap sensor gives +25 % for a 20 % gap change, while the differential one gives exactly 10 % for a 10 % move: the reason the differential form is preferred.

bank.q: An LVDT has a sensitivity of 40 mV per mm per volt of excitation. It is excited at 5 V rms. Find the output for a core displacement of 3 mm and state its phase relative to the excitation. Also find the displacement when the output reads 0.5 V rms.
outline: Sensitivity per volt = 40 mV/mm, excitation 5 V, so 200 mV/mm
3 mm gives 0.6 V rms
In-phase or 180° out of phase depending on which side of null
0.5 V corresponds to 2.5 mm
answer: Given. Sensitivity per volt of excitation S = 40 mV/(mm·V); excitation Vexc = 5 V rms; displacement x = 3 mm; then an output of 0.5 V rms.
Step 1: sensitivity at this excitation. K = S × Vexc = 40 mV/(mm·V) × 5 V = 200 mV/mm = 0.20 V/mm. A per-volt rating must always be multiplied by the actual drive before use.
Step 2: output at 3 mm. Vout = K·x = 0.20 V/mm × 3 mm = 0.60 V rms.

Step 3: phase. If the core has moved toward the secondary that is wound in the same sense as the output reference (call it S₁), Vout is in phase with the excitation (0°). If it has moved 3 mm the other way, the magnitude is still 0.60 V rms but the phase is 180°. In practice a small extra phase shift, a few degrees, appears from the winding inductance and resistance; the demodulator reference is trimmed to match.

Step 4: displacement for 0.5 V. x = Vout/K = 0.5/0.20 = 2.5 mm. The magnitude alone cannot say which side of null: 2.5 mm toward S₁ (in phase) or toward S₂ (antiphase). A phase-sensitive demodulator gives +2.5 mm or −2.5 mm.

Practical checks. The 3 mm must lie inside the rated linear range; if the LVDT is rated ±2.5 mm, the 3 mm reading is beyond it and the output will fall below 0.60 V. The residual voltage at null, say 5 mV, corresponds to 5/200 = 0.025 mm, which sets the useful resolution unless the demodulator rejects it. Doubling the excitation to 10 V would double K to 0.40 V/mm, but also the heating of the primary.

Direction-sensitive reading. After a phase-sensitive demodulator and low-pass filter the output becomes a DC voltage with a sign: +3 mm gives +0.60 V, −3 mm gives −0.60 V, and the 0.5 V reading becomes +0.5 V or −0.5 V, that is +2.5 mm or −2.5 mm. Plotted against x this is one straight line through zero with slope 0.20 V/mm, whereas an rms meter shows a V shape.
Check. 0.20 V/mm × 2.5 mm = 0.5 V, and 0.60/0.5 = 3/2.5 = 1.2, as the linear law requires.

bank.q: A parallel-plate capacitive displacement sensor has plates of area 25 cm² separated by 1 mm of air. Calculate the capacitance. If the gap is reduced to 0.5 mm, find the new capacitance and the percentage change. Comment on linearity.
outline: C = ε₀εᵣA/d with ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m
At 0.5 mm, C ≈ 44 pF
Change is 100%, not proportional to gap change
C ∝ 1/d, so gap type is non-linear; push-pull differential arrangement is used
answer: Given. A = 25 cm² = 25 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m²; d = 1 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m; air, εr = 1; ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
Percentage change. (44.27 − 22.13)/22.13 × 100 = +100 %. The gap fell by 50 %, but the capacitance doubled.

answer.text: Linearity. C ∝ 1/d, so equal gap steps do not give equal capacitance steps:

answer: The sensitivity dC/dd = −ε₀A/d² is −22.1 pF/mm at 1 mm and −88.5 pF/mm at 0.5 mm, four times larger. For a small movement Δd the fractional change is ΔC/C ≈ −Δd/d (a 1 % gap change gives about 1 %), but a 50 % change gives 100 %.

How it is linearised. (i) Keep the movement a small fraction of d. (ii) Use the differential three-plate form, where (C₁ − C₂)/(C₁ + C₂) = x/d exactly. (iii) Read the impedance 1/(ωC) instead of C: it is proportional to d, so a constant-current AC drive gives a voltage linear in gap. (iv) Linearise in software.

answer.text: Reading the gap linearly. Drive the sensor with a constant AC current of 10 µA at 10 kHz and measure the voltage across it:
answer.pre:
X = 1/(2πfC)
At 1.0 mm: X = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 22.13 × 10⁻¹²) = 719.0 kΩ → V = 10 µA × 719.0 kΩ = 7.19 V
At 0.5 mm: X = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 44.27 × 10⁻¹²) = 359.5 kΩ → V = 3.60 V
V/d = 7.19 V/mm in both cases: the voltage is proportional to the gap

answer: So the same sensor that gives a +100 % capacitance change gives an exactly halved voltage when the gap halves. The catch is the very high impedance, hundreds of kilohms, which makes the reading sensitive to cable capacitance and leakage.
Check on stray capacitance. A 1 m cable of about 100 pF is four times the 22 pF sensor; without a driven shield the cable would dominate.

bank.q: A steel gear with 40 teeth rotates at 600 rpm. Select the type of proximity sensor for counting teeth, state the required switching frequency, and explain how the sensor is wired to a PLC using a PNP normally-open output.
outline: Inductive proximity sensor, flush (shielded) mount for metal target
Tooth frequency = 40 × 600/60 = 400 pulses per second
Sensor switching frequency must exceed 400 Hz with margin
PNP NO: sensor switches +24 V to PLC input; PLC input common is 0 V (sinking input)
Hysteresis and repeatability decide pulse integrity at speed
Non-flush gives longer range but more side sensing
answer: Choice of sensor. The target is steel teeth, so an inductive proximity sensor is the natural choice: steel gives the full rated distance (K = 1), it ignores oil and swarf that would upset a capacitive sensor, and it has no moving parts. A flush (shielded) type can sit in a steel housing near the gear without sensing the housing.

answer.pre:
Speed = 600 rev/min = 600/60 = 10 rev/s
Pulse rate = 40 teeth × 10 rev/s = 400 pulses/s = 400 Hz
Period = 1/400 = 2.5 ms; with equal tooth and gap, ON for 1.25 ms

answer: The sensor’s rated switching frequency must exceed 400 Hz with margin; allow at least 50 %, i.e. 600 Hz or more. Inductive sensors are rated from a few hundred hertz to several kilohertz, so check the datasheet figure, which is measured with standard targets spaced at twice the sensor diameter.

Geometry. The sensing face must be smaller than a tooth and the gap between teeth, or the sensor sees two teeth at once and never switches off. Set the air gap to about half the rated distance, for example 2 mm for a 4 mm sensor, so wear and runout do not move the tooth out of range.

Wiring a PNP normally-open output. Three wires (standard colours): brown to +24 V DC, blue to 0 V, black is the output. When a tooth is present the PNP transistor switches the black wire to +24 V (sourcing). It goes to a PLC input of the sinking type, whose common is tied to 0 V, so current flows from the sensor, through the input, to 0 V. NO means the output is ON only while a tooth is present.

PLC side. 1.25 ms pulses are shorter than a typical PLC scan of 5–20 ms, so an ordinary input would miss most of them. The sensor must go to a high-speed counter input, which counts in hardware; speed = counted pulses per second ÷ 40 teeth.

head: Item
Choice
rows: PNP, NO; brown +24 V, blue 0 V, black to input

answer: Integrity at speed. Hysteresis stops chatter at the tooth edge; repeatability keeps the pulse width steady. A non-flush sensor would reach farther but also see the gear face and nearby metal.
Check. 400 pulses/s ÷ 40 teeth = 10 rev/s × 60 = 600 rev/min, recovering the given speed.

bank.q: A capacitive pressure sensor uses a diaphragm of area 100 mm² and gap 20 μm. Find the capacitance. If full-scale pressure deflects the diaphragm by 2 μm, find the capacitance at full scale and the sensitivity in pF per μm.
outline: C = ε₀A/d with A = 100 × 10⁻⁶ m² and d = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m: C = 44.27 pF
At 18 µm: C = 49.19 pF
Average sensitivity over the 2 µm = 4.92/2 = 2.46 pF/µm; the slope at 20 µm is C/d = 2.21 pF/µm
The two differ because C ∝ 1/d: sensitivity rises as the gap closes
Small deflection keeps the response near-linear; a differential layout linearises it
answer: Given. A = 100 mm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², d = 20 µm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, air; full-scale deflection 2 µm. Treat the diaphragm as a flat plate moving as a piston (a real diaphragm bows, so this is an upper estimate).

answer.pre:
Average over the 2 µm: 4.92 pF/2 µm = 2.46 pF/µm
At rest (slope):      dC/dx = C₀/d = 44.27/20 = 2.21 pF/µm
At full scale:        C/d′ = 49.19/18 = 2.73 pF/µm

answer: The sensitivity rises by 24 % across the range because C ∝ 1/(d − x). The small-change formula ΔC ≈ C₀·x/d = 44.27 × 0.1 = 4.43 pF is 10 % low at full scale.
Signal size. With a charge amplifier, Vp = 5 V and Cf = 50 pF, full scale gives Vp·ΔC/Cf = 5 × 4.92/50 = 0.49 V.

Keeping it linear. Limit the deflection to a small part of d (here 10 %), use a differential two-gap sensor with the diaphragm between two fixed electrodes, or linearise digitally using the known 1/(d − x) law.

answer.text: Differential version. Put the diaphragm midway between two fixed electrodes, each 20 µm away. Full-scale pressure moves it 2 µm toward one and away from the other:

answer: The differential ratio equals x/d at every point, so a pressure sensor built this way, as in many medical and process transmitters, needs no linearising.
Check. C·d is constant: 44.27 × 20 = 49.19 × 18 = 885 pF·µm.

bank.q: Compare inductive, LVDT, eddy current and capacitive transducers for displacement measurement under the headings: range, linearity, contact, sensitivity to environment, cost and typical application.
outline: LVDT: mm to hundreds of mm, very linear, no contact, robust, costlier
Variable reluctance: small range, non-linear, cheap, needs bridge
Eddy current: small gap, non-contact, needs conducting target, sensitive to conductivity
Capacitive: small range, very high resolution, affected by humidity and stray capacitance
Selection depends on target material, environment and resolution needed
Give one industrial and one biomedical example, such as roll-gap measurement and tendon-specimen extension
answer: Approach. Compare a single-coil variable reluctance sensor, an LVDT, an eddy current probe and a capacitive sensor under each heading, with typical values.

head: Heading
Variable reluctance
LVDT
Eddy current
Capacitive
rows: very robust; sealed versions for oil and radiation
works through oil and dirt; needs conducting target
upset by humidity, dirt, stray capacitance

answer: Variable reluctance. In the chapter’s example a 20 % gap change gives only a 16.7 % change in L, showing the 1/g law; a push-pull pair gives a linear (Vs/2)·x/g. Simple and cheap, it suits short-range industrial and respiratory-pressure duties.

LVDT. The best general-purpose choice: linear, frictionless, infinite resolution and long life. Example: 0.24 V/mm at 3 V, ±2.5 mm, linearity ±6.25 µm. It needs AC excitation and a phase-sensitive demodulator, and the core and rod add mass.

Eddy current. Ideal where nothing can be attached to the target, such as a rotating shaft: −2.5 V/mm over a few millimetres, bandwidth of kilohertz. Calibration changes with the target metal, and the target must be thicker than about 3 skin depths.
Capacitive. The highest resolution and lowest force on the object, but a 2 pF sensor beside 100 pF of cable needs guarding, and humidity changes εr. The differential form gives exactly x/d.

Selection. Ask four questions: is the target conducting (eddy current possible)? Can something be attached (LVDT, reluctance)? Is nanometre resolution needed in a clean place (capacitive)? Is the environment hot, oily or wet (LVDT or eddy current)?

Examples. Industrial: roll-gap and strip-thickness gauging in a rolling mill uses LVDTs; turbine shaft vibration uses eddy current probes. Biomedical: tendon and bone specimen extension in a test machine uses an LVDT; ventilator and lung-function pressure sensors use capacitive or variable-reluctance diaphragms.
Check. Only the LVDT and the differential forms give a straight-line output over the whole range without software correction.

bank.q: A plant reports an LVDT reading that does not return to zero when the core returns to the mechanical null. Evaluate the possible causes and the corrections.
outline: Residual voltage from winding mismatch, stray capacitance, harmonics
Core not at electrical null; mechanical zero differs from electrical zero
Excitation frequency drift and phase shift in demodulator
Temperature change in windings and former
Corrections: null adjustment, phase-sensitive demodulation, stable oscillator, shielding, calibration at zero and full scale
answer: The symptom. The core is back at the mechanical zero, but the reading is not zero. Separate the possible causes into electrical (the output at the true null is not zero) and mechanical (the core is not at the true null).

Cause 1: residual voltage. Winding asymmetry between S₁ and S₂, harmonics in the excitation and stray capacitance between primary and secondaries leave a few millivolts at null. With K = 0.50 V/mm, 5 mV reads as 0.010 mm. Much of the residual is in quadrature (90°) or at harmonic frequencies. Correction: a phase-sensitive demodulator, which rejects the quadrature part and harmonics; a null-balancing network; a pure sine excitation; earthed shield.

Cause 2: mechanical zero is not the electrical null. The fixture may have shifted, or the core rod may have slipped in its clamp. Thermal expansion also moves it: a 100 mm steel bracket warming by 20 °C grows 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 20 = 0.024 mm, which reads as 0.024 × 0.50 = 12 mV. Correction: re-zero by finding the minimum-output position, lock the core, use brackets of low-expansion material or symmetric mounting.

Cause 3: demodulator phase error. If the demodulator reference is not in phase with the signal, part of the quadrature residual leaks into the DC output and the zero shifts. A phase shift that changes with excitation frequency or temperature makes the zero drift. Correction: trim the reference phase at the working frequency, and use a stable crystal or ratiometric oscillator.

Cause 4: excitation or temperature drift. Temperature changes the copper resistance of the primary, so the primary current and K drift; if the secondaries warm unequally the null itself moves. Correction: constant-current or ratiometric excitation (read Vout/(V₁ + V₂)), temperature-compensated LVDT, allow warm-up.

Cause 5: hysteresis in the mechanism. Friction or backlash in the linkage that drives the core means the core stops short when returning. The LVDT itself has no friction. Correction: approach zero from one direction, fix the linkage, use spring-loaded probes.
Cause 6: interference and earthing. Pickup from nearby motors or ground loops adds an offset. Correction: shielded twisted cable, single-point earth, filter.

Procedure. Disconnect the mechanism and find the LVDT’s own null with a scope: if the minimum is a few millivolts and mostly 90° out of phase, the electronics are at fault; if the minimum is at a different core position, the mechanics are. Then calibrate at zero and full scale.

bank.q: Compare an LVDT-based diaphragm pressure gauge with a capacitive pressure sensor for measuring 0 to 100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O (about 0 to 10 kPa) of airway pressure in a ventilator. Which would you choose and why?
outline: LVDT type: robust, large output, but a moving core and linkage, more mass and slower
Capacitive: small, high resolution, fast, low moving mass, but a few pF needs a charge amplifier and guarding
Capacitive needs temperature compensation and linearisation of the 1/d law
Both read the diaphragm without contact; both must survive coughs and overpressure
Choose the capacitive sensor for a ventilator: size, speed and cost; justify clearly
answer: Requirement. 0 to 100 cmH2O is 0 to 9.81 kPa (1 cmH2O = 98.07 Pa). Resolution about 0.1 cmH2O, response fast enough for breaths up to about 60 per minute in neonates and their harmonics (tens of hertz), small size, low cost, survives coughs and overpressure.

LVDT-based gauge. A diaphragm or bellows drives the LVDT core. To use an LVDT well the core should move about a millimetre at full scale: with 0.5 V/mm that gives 0.5 V. At under 10 kPa that needs a large, soft diaphragm or bellows. Merits: robust, high output, infinite resolution, well-proven. Demerits: the core, rod and large diaphragm add mass, so the natural frequency is low and the response slow; bigger, heavier and dearer; needs AC excitation and a demodulator.

Capacitive sensor. The diaphragm is itself one plate. In the chapter’s example A = 4 mm², d = 5 µm, 0.02 µm per cmH2O: C rises from 7.08 pF to 7.70 pF at 20 cmH2O and 11.81 pF at 100 cmH2O, giving 0.31 V and 2.36 V from a charge amplifier (Vp = 5 V, Cf = 10 pF). Deflections are micrometres, so the diaphragm is light and fast. Merits: small, high resolution, fast, low power, cheap in volume as a silicon or ceramic die. Demerits: picofarad signal needs a charge amplifier or capacitance-to-digital converter at the sensor; the 1/d law needs linearisation (the small-change formula is 40 % low at 100 cmH2O in that example); temperature and humidity must be compensated.

head: Heading
LVDT diaphragm gauge
Capacitive sensor
rows: LVDT linear; diaphragm may not be

answer: Common points. Both read the diaphragm without contact; both need a gauge port vented to atmosphere and protection against moisture from the breathing circuit (a filter or hydrophobic membrane).

Choice. The capacitive sensor. In a ventilator the decisive points are speed for waveform display and trigger detection, small size, and cost; the capacitive sensor wins on all three, and its non-linearity is removed by the digital calibration the ventilator already performs. An LVDT gauge would suit a larger, slower process measurement where robustness matters more.
Check. 100 cmH2O × 0.02 µm = 2 µm of deflection, 40 % of the 5 µm gap: well inside the plates but large enough that linearisation is needed.

bank.q: A proximity sensor in a press safety guard trips intermittently. Analyse the likely causes using the ideas of sensing range, hysteresis, repeatability, flush mounting and output type.
outline: Target distance near the edge of nominal range, so hysteresis and repeatability matter
Non-flush mounting causes side sensing of nearby metal
Wrong output type (PNP vs NPN) or NO vs NC wiring against the load
Supply ripple, cable length and electrical noise from the press
Speed of approach against switching frequency
Fixes: correct mounting, margin of 60–80% of range, screening, correct polarity
answer: Set-up. Take an inductive sensor with Sn = 8 mm watching a steel flag on the guard door, NC output to a safety relay. “Trips intermittently” means the output sometimes drops although the door is shut.

Cause 1: target near the edge of range. The real switching distance lies between 0.9 and 1.1 Sn, and the assured operating distance is about 0.81 Sn = 6.5 mm across temperature and supply. If the flag sits at 7.0 mm (87.5 % of Sn), small changes take it out of range. Door vibration of ±0.5 mm moves it between 6.5 and 7.5 mm. Fix: set the target at 50–80 % of Sn (4–6.5 mm), or choose a larger sensor.

Cause 2: hysteresis and repeatability. Hysteresis (often up to 15 % of the switching distance) makes release farther than operate, which helps; but if the target hovers near the release point, repeatability scatter of a few percent makes the output toggle. Fix: move the target well inside so both edges are clear.

Cause 3: target material. A stainless or aluminium flag has K well below 1 (e.g. 0.5 for brass, 0.4 for aluminium), so the effective distance shrinks to 3–4 mm. Fix: use a mild-steel flag or recompute S = K·Sn.

Cause 4: flush mounting. A non-flush sensor sunk into a steel bracket sees the bracket and changes its switching point with the bracket’s position and temperature. Fix: use a flush (shielded) sensor in metal, or give a non-flush one its required free zone.

Cause 5: output type and wiring. A PNP sensor on a sourcing input (or NPN on sinking) gives no reliable signal; a loose terminal or a cable flexing in the door hinge breaks intermittently. With an NC circuit a break trips the guard, which is safe but shows up as nuisance trips. Fix: match PNP to sinking inputs, use flexible cable and strain relief, check terminals.

Cause 6: supply and noise. A press creates large switching transients and supply dips; ripple beyond the rated limit, or noise coupled into a long unshielded cable, can make the sensor or input glitch. Fix: separate the sensor cable from motor cables, keep the supply within ripple limits, add filtering.

Cause 7: speed. A door that bounces or approaches fast may pass faster than the sensor’s response time; with a switching frequency of several hundred hertz this is rarely the issue but should be checked.

Diagnosis. Watch the sensor LED while shaking the shut door; measure the target gap with feeler gauges; log trips against press strokes. For a safety function, a coded safety switch or a sensor rated for safety duty is the proper final fix.

bank.q: Explain why the capacitor microphone needs a high-impedance preamplifier and a polarising voltage. Compare its signal-conditioning needs with those of a capacitive pressure sensor.
outline: Fixed charge q = CV, so V = q/C; a small gap change gives a voltage change
Very small capacitance (tens of pF) means very high source impedance
Preamplifier must have high input impedance and low input capacitance, placed close to the capsule
Polarising voltage (or electret charge) is needed to set q
Pressure sensor may use a charge amplifier or AC bridge with synchronous demodulation
Both need guarding and shielding against stray capacitance
answer: Polarising voltage. The microphone is a capacitor whose diaphragm moves with sound. A change in C produces an electrical signal only if there is charge on the plates. A polarising voltage Vp applied through a very large resistor sets the charge q = C·Vp; an electret supplies the charge permanently instead.

answer.text: Constant charge gives a voltage. The bias resistor is so large that, at audio frequencies, q cannot change quickly. Then V = q/C = q·d/(ε₀A), so the voltage is proportional to the gap:
answer.pre:
ΔV/V<sub>p</sub> = Δd/d
Example: V<sub>p</sub> = 50 V, d = 20 µm, deflection 0.020 µm
ΔV = 50 × 0.020/20 = 0.050 V = 50 mV

answer.text: Why a high-impedance preamplifier. The capsule of the chapter’s example is only 11.07 pF. Its impedance is huge:

answer: Any load resistance comparable with these drains the charge and cuts the bass. The bias resistor R and C form a high-pass filter, f = 1/(2πRC): R = 1 GΩ gives f = 14 Hz, just enough for audio. So the preamplifier (a JFET or op-amp buffer) must have an input resistance in the gigaohms and a very small input capacitance.

Cable capacitance. In this voltage mode a 1 m cable of 100 pF sits in parallel with the 11.07 pF capsule and divides the signal: 11.07/(11.07 + 100) = 0.10, a loss of 90 %. That is why the preamplifier is built into the microphone body, right behind the capsule.

Capacitive pressure sensor: needs. It must measure static pressure, down to DC, so the constant-charge trick fails (the charge leaks away through the bias resistor). Instead it uses AC excitation at 1–100 kHz with a bridge or a capacitance-to-voltage converter, followed by synchronous (phase-sensitive) demodulation, or a charge amplifier with a switched or AC drive. The output is a DC voltage proportional to pressure, linearised for the 1/d law.

head: Need
Capacitor microphone
Capacitive pressure sensor
rows: GΩ input buffer at the capsule
removed by driven shield or virtual ground

answer: Common to both. Picofarad capacitances, so guarding and shielding, short leads at the sensor, and protection of the diaphragm from moisture and overpressure.

Check. 50 mV for a 0.1 % gap change at 50 V bias is a usable signal, but a 100 MΩ input would raise the low cut-off to 1/(2π × 10⁸ × 11.07 × 10⁻¹²) = 144 Hz and lose the bass: the front end must be gigaohm and sit at the capsule.

glossary.def: The opposition a magnetic circuit offers to flux, equal to length divided by permeability times area.
The non-magnetic part of a magnetic path, whose reluctance is large and changes with mechanical movement.
The flux linkage produced in one coil by unit current in another coil.
A transducer whose inductance changes because a mechanical input changes the reluctance of its magnetic path.
A transformer with one primary and two opposed secondaries whose differential output is proportional to core displacement.
The core position at the centre of an LVDT where the two secondary EMFs cancel and the output is zero.
The small output left at null because the two secondaries are not perfectly identical.
A circuit that converts the AC output of an inductive transducer into a DC voltage whose sign shows direction.
A rotary transformer whose output amplitude varies with the shaft angle of its rotor.
A rotary electromagnetic device that transmits or compares shaft angles between two places over wires.
A synchro used as a receiver that outputs a voltage proportional to the angular error between two shafts.
A small, sensitive rotary variable-reluctance pick-off used for fine angle and rate measurement.
Current induced in a conductor by a changing magnetic field, flowing in closed loops that oppose the change.
The depth to which an alternating field penetrates a conductor, decreasing as frequency and conductivity rise.
A non-contact switch that changes state when a target comes within its sensing range.
The distance at which a proximity sensor reliably switches for a stated standard target.
The difference between the switch-on and switch-off distances of a proximity sensor.
How closely a sensor switches at the same distance on repeated approaches.
A proximity sensor with a metal shield that can be mounted level with a metal surface without false operation.
A sensor output that switches the positive supply to the load, used with sinking PLC inputs.
The charge stored per unit volt, C = ε₀εᵣA/d for a parallel-plate capacitor.
A three-plate capacitor whose two halves change in opposite directions, giving a linear output.
A circuit that converts charge from a capacitive sensor into a voltage independent of cable capacitance.
A conductor held at the same potential as a sensor plate to remove stray field and stray capacitance effects.
A permanently charged dielectric used in capacitor microphones to avoid an external polarising supply.
Breathing measurement from the self inductance of wire loops in elastic belts round the chest and abdomen.
Two sensing elements that change in opposite directions with the measurand, giving a linear output and cancelling common drifts.
